label: paragraph_title
text: GETTING TOGETHER

label: text
text: Pecksniffian as it may seem, there is at least one thing to be counted to us for righteousness. The Pharisees thanked God he was not as other men even as this Publican. We may reasonably thank God we are not as other men in the dispute in which we are unwilling but determined participants. There has been no reciprocity. Whilst Britishers have suffered affront, insult, and in some cases have been in danger of their lives, the Chinese

label: text
text: in Hongkong—with the exception of the loafer, the intimidator and the lawless—have pursued what may be described as “the eventenor of their ways.” The merchant is not reviled, nor are shopkeepers’ windows smashed. We still hold friendly converse with those of our Chinese friends and acquaintances whom we have learned to regard, and in whose sanity we have every hope and confidence. We are, pharisical as it may sound not as the extremists of the other side who juggle with lies as they do with principles — surpassing well. It may seem strange that this phase of British temperament has not been more effective in bringing things to a state of settlement. It may be comforting to think that its effect will be all to the good, even if the result will be delayed somewhat. Unfortunately it is impossible to get this effect to Canton where the aforesaid juggling of lies, on those all too willing to believe them, is having a contra effect. In the good time which we firmly believe is coming when the lion will lie down with the lamb, there should once more be a resurrection of the various suggestions made to get the Colony’s wide and varied nationalities known more to each other. A League of Fellowship and Service might have done something to that end. But the slingers of hackneyisms, and with an outlook almost blinded by mind instigmatism, found Kipling’s undisputed geographical formulae that East is East, and West is West, with the contentious addendum that the twain were never meant to, or would not meet, a trite saying to bolster up their arguments. The idea that peoples of different hues and creeds are, as a result, unable to meet in fellowship and service, must, to the serious minded, to like the peace that passeth all understanding. A suggestion of

label: text
text: It cannot possibly attach itself to the suggestion of an International Club. The very name is so suggestive of its intent, that space need not be taken up in arguing in its favour. Neither a League nor a Club is likely to bring in the millennium, or settle a strike or an outbreak. It would be foolish to make this claim for them. But, in the case of a Club, it would afford a means for those who, in the main, are responsible for the "life-blood" of the Colony—its trade and commerce—getting into touch one with the other, and so lessening the feeling of cold and studied isolation, making one party lean to the opinion that so far as business is concerned, he and his conferees, were all right, but after that they faded from the scheme of things. Perhaps a thought will be given to the possibilities here suggested when the normal comes to be our daily lot again.

label: paragraph_title
text: Learning Malay.

label: text
text: We started away in Indian file. That is to say, I had one man in front of me; then I came; then the coolies, carrying my baggage.... Finally we reached a river and found two boats waiting for us. The Malays built sunshades over the boats and placed a mattress at the bottom of my boat, and off we went.

label: text
text: The boat was a very gracefully carved dugout, about twenty-five feet long and three feet wide. The deck was made of strips of bamboo, and in the bow were running boards for the four coolies who poled the boat. In the stern was a kajang, or roofed structure, underneath which I lay in comfort, upon a mattress, with the kamudi, or steersman, behind me. As I couldn't speak the Malay language, I felt extraordinarily helpless with six Malays who couldn't speak a word of English. The sixth was a young fellow about seventeen called Sahar, the colour of chocolate, with straight black hair, beautiful teeth, and dressed in a most gorgeous silk sarong.

label: text
text: Sahar eyed me all over, then said something in Malay which caused roars of laughter. Suddenly, I remembered that I knew two words of the Malay language: upa, menning "what," and nama, meaning "name." So I got out a pencil and notebook and, pointing at the water, I said, Apa nama?" Sahar immediately said. "Ayer." I hurriedly scribbled down in my little book, "Water-ayer." Then I touched a piece of wood and said, "Apanama?" And Sahar said, "Kayou," and again I wrote down in my little book, "Wood-kayou." Then I touched Sahar's head, and I said, "Kayou!" The four other Malays roared with laughter and I appreciated at once that my joke had amply repaid me for the joke Sahar had had at my expense: in fact, already I could joke in Malay! As a matter of fact, with the aid of those two words, apanama, I acquired an excellent vocabulary, and I discovered that by stringing the words together in the same order as English I could, usually make myself understood. Of course, it took me several years to speak Malay even very poorly, but only a few hours to make myself understood.—Carveth Wells, in "Six Years in the Malay Jungle."

label: paragraph_title

label: text
text: (To the Editor of the P. & T. Times.)

label: text
text: Read one paper and you become prejudiced read all and you become mad Mr. P. M. Oliver

label: text
text: Sir,—May I, through your columns, thank the full military band which, from a very early hour, played with such enthusiasm beneath my bedroom window in the Hongkong Road district this morning. How they ascertained that it was the occasion of my birthday is a mystery to me, but it was a kindly thought to aid me to enjoy one hour more of so auspicious a day. I am afraid I did not trouble to get out of bed to see who my unknown friends were, as I was fully engaged in keeping the children from crying, and so I trust they will take this as sufficient acknowledgment.

label: text
text: I shall not be having a birthday next year.

label: text
text: Yours faithfully:

label: text
text: In view of what has taken place, the last five words are particularly noteworthy:—

label: text
text: Quite striking is the characterisation of the Canton Christian College, at Canton, China, by Philip N. Youtz, a former member of its teaching staff, in Current History Magazine, as a “powerful broadcasting station for modern thought, as well as a model of higher living.” The college is not entirely a foreign institution, as it is conducted jointly by Chinese and American educators, the professors on the faculty representing no less than fifteen denominations, thirty American and European universities and two races. It is hence with no little interest that one reads that in this institution may be found “many of the finest traditions and customs of American university life adapted to the needs of awakening. China.” This awakening of China is without doubt destined to be one of the great events of the near future, and when it is realised that the boys who graduate from the various departments will contribute much to it, a feeling of satisfaction may be felt that it is in good hands.

label: text
text: The doctors in their general assembly have been considering ways and in xins of abolishing the quick, observes the "Daily Telegraph" (London). It was proposed to seek such an amendment of the Medical Acts that no person without the accepted professional qualification should be allowed to practise medicine or surgery. To this answer was made that by so stringent a rule the chemist would be forbidden to offer a draught of carbonate of soda or full volatile, the helpful friend to recommend the régime which he had himself found grateful and comforting. This public, we must allow, would not submit to these restrictions, and, no doubt, the assembly did wisely to do nothing. But a good deal of sympathy will be felt, and should be felt, with the complaint against quacks. We have no difficulty in believing Dr. Manon's stories of the impudence of modern quackery, and we quite agree with him that many people are sent to jail for offences much less serious than those committed by these unqualified practitioners. The offence of obtaining money under false preferences is in fact, only a small part of the injury done by the quack. He destroys confidence in the scientific treatment of disease and thus incalculably increases suffering and loss. Patients who might have been cured remain under his hands till it is too late or till he has aggravated the evil. Many foolish people are persuaded that the quack has some mysterious power denied to science, and when ill-nec�as come, try anything rather than rations treatment. label: text
text: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog, who have had always with us, and probably we always shall. There will always be people who expect to be cured by magic, who prefer the charlitan's promise of swift and easy salvation to the slow and difficult processes of medical treatment; and until medical science has solved all its problems, there is a strong temptation to believe that the plausible empiric has hit upon the secret which is hidden from the orthodox practitioners. The vogue of the quick is the consequence of the nature of man. But we may venture to hint that the medical profession without laws or regulations could make it more difficult than it is for him to find votaries. Let them with individual patients and the general public avoid all unnecessary mystery, talk a language understood by the ordinary man, and trust him with as much information as possible about his own case, and the power of medical science in such cases. The antidote to quickens and quackery is knowledge.
